title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 1
paragraphs: History is the life of nations and of humanity. To capture and put into words—to directly describe—the life of humanity or even of a single nation seems impossible.

The ancient historians all used one and the same method to describe and capture the apparently elusive life of a people. They described the activities of individuals who ruled the people, and treated those activities as representing the activity of the whole nation.

The question of how individuals made nations act according to their will, and what guided the will of those individuals themselves, the ancients answered by invoking a divinity that subjected nations to the will of a chosen man and guided that man's will toward a predetermined end.
For the ancients, these questions were resolved by belief in the direct involvement of God in human affairs.
Modern history, in theory, rejects both these principles.

It would seem that, having rejected the ancients' belief in humanity's subjection to God and in a predetermined goal toward which nations are led, modern history should study not the displays of power but the causes that produce it. But modern history has not done this. Having rejected the theoretical views of the ancients, it follows them in practice.

Instead of men endowed with divine authority and directly guided by God's will, modern history has given us either heroes with extraordinary, superhuman abilities, or simply men of various kinds—from monarchs to journalists—who lead the masses. Instead of the ancients' divinely appointed goals for nations—the greatness of Rome, Greece, or God's chosen people—modern history has set up its own goals: the welfare of the French, German, or English people, or—in its highest abstraction—the welfare and civilization of all humanity, by which it usually means the peoples occupying a small northwestern corner of a large continent.

Modern history has rejected the ancients' beliefs without replacing them with a new understanding, and the logic of the situation has forced historians—after apparently rejecting the divine authority of kings and the "destiny" of the ancients—to arrive at the same conclusion by a different road: to recognize (1) that nations are led by individual people, and (2) that there exists a certain goal toward which nations and humanity are being guided.
All the works of modern historians, from Gibbon to Buckle, despite their apparent disagreements and seeming novelty of outlook, rest on those two old, inescapable assumptions.

In the first place, the historian describes the activity of individuals who in his opinion directed humanity. One historian considers only monarchs, generals, and ministers as such people, while another includes orators, scholars, reformers, philosophers, and poets as well. But all historians agree that these individuals expressed the will of their time, and that their activity was the direction in which the historical movement flowed.

In 1789 a ferment arises in Paris; it grows, spreads, and takes the form of a movement of peoples from west to east. Several times it surges eastward and collides with a counter-movement from east to west. In 1812 it reaches its extreme limit—Moscow—and then, with remarkable symmetry, a counter-movement occurs from east to west, pulling along the peoples of Central Europe. The counter-movement reaches the starting point—Paris—and subsides.

During those twenty years, an immense number of fields were left untilled, houses were burned, trade changed direction, millions of people migrated, were impoverished or enriched, and millions of Christian men who professed the law of love slaughtered one another.

What does all this mean? Why did it happen? What made those people burn houses and kill their fellow men? What were the causes of these events? What force made people act this way? These are the instinctive, simple, and most natural questions humanity asks when it encounters the monuments and traditions of that bygone era.
For answers to these questions, common sense turns to the science of history, whose purpose is to help nations and humanity know themselves.

If history had kept the ancients' conception, it would have said: God, to reward or punish His people, gave Napoleon power and directed his will toward the fulfillment of divine purposes. And that answer would have been clear and complete. One could believe or disbelieve in the divine significance of Napoleon, but for anyone who believed in it, all of that era's history would have been comprehensible, and there would be no contradictions.
But modern history cannot give that answer. Science does not accept the ancients' belief in direct divine intervention in human affairs, and therefore history must provide different answers.
Modern history, answering these questions, says: you want to know what this movement means, what caused it, and what force produced these events? Listen:

"Louis XIV was a very proud and self-confident man; he had such-and-such mistresses and such-and-such ministers, and he ruled France badly. His successors were weak men and they too ruled France badly. And they had certain favorites and certain mistresses. Furthermore, at that time certain men wrote certain books. At the end of the eighteenth century, about twenty men got together in Paris and started saying that all men are equal and free. This led people all over France to start attacking and killing each other. They killed the king and many others. At that time there was a man of genius in France—Napoleon. He conquered everyone everywhere—that is, he killed a lot of people—because he was a very great genius. And for some reason he went to kill Africans, and killed them so well, and was so cunning and clever, that when he returned to France he ordered everyone to obey him. And they all obeyed him. Having become an Emperor, he went to kill people in Italy, Austria, and Prussia. And there too he killed a great many. In Russia there was Emperor Alexander, who decided to restore order in Europe and therefore fought against Napoleon. But in 1807 he suddenly made friends with Napoleon, then in 1811 quarreled with him again, and again they went about killing a great many people. Napoleon led six hundred thousand men into Russia and captured Moscow; then he suddenly ran away from Moscow, and Emperor Alexander—aided by the advice of Stein and others—united Europe to march against the destroyer of its peace. All Napoleon's allies suddenly became his enemies; and this force marched against Napoleon, who had raised fresh forces. The allies defeated Napoleon, entered Paris, forced Napoleon to abdicate, and sent him to the island of Elba, without depriving him of his title of Emperor and showing him every respect, though five years before and one year later they all considered him a brigand and an outlaw. Then Louis XVIII—who until then had been an object of ridicule to both the French and the allies—began to reign. As for Napoleon, after shedding tears before the Old Guard, he abdicated and went into exile. Then skillful statesmen and diplomats (particularly Talleyrand, who managed to sit down before anyone else in a particular chair at a particular reception, thereby enlarging the borders of France) held talks in Vienna and by those talks made the nations happy or unhappy. Then the diplomats and monarchs nearly quarreled and were about to order their armies to kill each other once more; but at that moment Napoleon arrived back in France with a battalion, and the French, who had been hating him, all immediately submitted. But the allied monarchs were displeased at this and again went to fight the French. And the genius Napoleon was defeated and taken to the island of St. Helena, having suddenly been recognized as a robber. And there the exile, separated from his dear ones and from his beloved France, died a slow death on a rock and bequeathed his great deeds to posterity. But in Europe a reaction set in, and the sovereigns all took to oppressing their peoples again."

It would be wrong to think this is ironic—a caricature of historical accounts. On the contrary, it is a very mild rendering of the contradictory and inconclusive answers that all historians give, from the authors of memoirs and national histories to the writers of universal histories and the new cultural historians.
The strangeness and absurdity of these answers comes from the fact that modern history, like a deaf man, answers questions no one has asked.

If the purpose of history is to describe the movement of humanity and of nations, the first question—without answering which everything else becomes incomprehensible—is: What is the power that moves peoples? To this, modern history laboriously tells us that Napoleon was a very great genius, or that Louis XIV was very proud, or that certain writers wrote certain books.

All that may be so, and humanity is ready to agree. But it is not what was asked. All that would be interesting if we accepted a divine power, based on itself and always consistent, directing nations through Napoleons, Louises, and writers. But we do not accept such a power, and therefore, before talking about Napoleons, Louises, and writers, we need to show the connection between these individuals and the movement of nations.
If some other force has replaced divine power, then it should be explained what this new force consists of, because the whole interest of history lies precisely in that force.

History seems to assume that this force is self-evident and known to everyone. But despite every desire to regard it as known, anyone who reads many historical works cannot help doubting whether this new force—so differently understood by historians themselves—is really so well known to everyone.
